# Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents

Minhyeon Oh, Chiyeong Heo, Geonwoo Noh, Hoyoung Kim Email:
<minhyeon.oh@postech.ac.kr>    Jangwon Son, Jungseul OkPohang University
of Science and TechnologyNational AI Research Lab ^(†)^(†)thanks:
Corresponding author. Email: <jungseul.ok@postech.ac.kr>

###### Abstract

Language model agents increasingly act on users’ behalf by manipulating
external environments through tools, often from high-level instructions
that leave critical task- and environment-specific context unstated. To
prevent resulting misaligned actions, recent work verifies proposed
actions before execution, largely by establishing whether the conditions
supporting them hold. We argue that this confirmation-oriented view
leaves a fundamental blind spot: a wrong action often passes every check
that asks whether it is right. This motivates a different question for
verification: rather than asking what evidence supports an action, can
the agent find evidence that refutes it? We pursue this direction with
BlackSwan, a refutation-oriented, expect-suspect-test procedure that
predicts the intended effect of each state-mutating action, formulates
specific and empirically testable hypotheses for how it could be wrong,
and tests them using existing observations or additional non-mutating
actions, executing the action only if none survives testing. On
challenging AppWorld tasks, BlackSwan improves success rate over the
strongest baseline by 14.9 and 25.2%p with and without the backbone
model’s thinking mode, respectively. Even without thinking or in-context
demonstrations, it outperforms stronger baselines equipped with them.
The gains also transfer beyond AppWorld, with BlackSwan improving
WebShop performance by 12.7%p. More broadly, our results suggest that
language model agents have an underused capacity to recognize and
self-correct misaligned actions, which can be systematically elicited
through active conjecture and refutation before execution.

## 1 Introduction

A central promise of language model agents is that they can complete
delegated tasks autonomously: on behalf of users, they perceive and
manipulate user environments through tools ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib39); [Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib35); [Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib36)). Yet, in practice, users typically specify
high-level goals, leaving critical information implicit in their
environments ([Shah et al., 2019](#bib.bib21); [Trivedi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib29)). Worse, the user-specific environment states and
dynamics lie beyond an agent’s parametric knowledge ([Chae et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)). Faced with this information gap, agents may take
actions that deviate from the user’s actual intent ([Vijayvargiya et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib31); [Shayegani et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)). Unlike a
flawed chat response, which can simply be ignored, a flawed action
changes the environment itself, turning an incorrect inference about
unstated context into a potentially hard-to-reverse consequence.

One natural response to this information gap is to equip agents with
richer knowledge of their environments ([Fu et al., 2024](#bib.bib7);
[Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib4); [Wang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib37); [Zhang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib41); [Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib16); [Chen et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib3)). Yet user environments are open-ended: it is
difficult to know in advance which facts will matter to actions that
arise later in a task. Such up-front knowledge acquisition therefore
faces a basic question of sufficiency—when has the agent learned enough?

More recent work shifts the focus from understanding the environment in
general to verifying individual proposed actions on the fly ([Fang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Ning et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15); [Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib5); [Jiang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)). These methods intervene before execution and
establish whether task- and environment-specific conditions for the
action hold. This reflects a _confirmation-oriented_ view of action
readiness: ask what must be established for the proposed action to
proceed, then seek evidence for those conditions. But a wrong action can
pass every check that asks whether it is right. For example, asked to
“split last night’s dinner bill among the attendees”, an agent may
confirm the bill amount and the guest list on the event invitation, yet
miss that one invitee canceled by message.

In this work, we argue for a _refutation-oriented_ view ([Popper &
Hudson, 1963](#bib.bib17)) of preemptive action verification. The
central question is not merely how much evidence verification should
gather, but in which direction it should look: should it seek evidence
for an action, or evidence _against_ it? The confirmation-oriented view
takes the former, admitting an action once the conditions required to
support it are established. In contrast, the refutation-oriented view
takes the latter: it asks how the action _could be wrong_, constructs
potential falsifiers, and admits the action only if none survives
empirical scrutiny. The action is thus corroborated by withstanding
attempted refutation, rather than confirmed by accumulated support.

To operationalize this view, we propose BlackSwan¹¹ 1 The name alludes
to Popper’s classic black-swan example: observing more white swans
cannot verify that all swans are white, whereas a single black swan can
refute the claim., which subjects each state-mutating action to an
expect-suspect-test procedure: the action executes only if it withstands
the attempt to refute it; otherwise, it is withheld, and the agent
drafts a replacement in light of the refuting evidence. Specifically,
expect predicts what the proposed action itself would accomplish toward
the user’s task, yielding an action-local claim that can be challenged
without conflating failures of the current write with unfinished parts
of the task. Given this claim, suspect raises specific, empirically
testable hypotheses about how it could be wrong. We keep this stage
separate from testing, following the principle that hypotheses must not
depend on the data used to test them ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)):
if hypotheses were formulated while evidence is gathered, the evidence
could shape the very hypotheses it is then used to adjudicate. Finally,
test tries to refute the action by seeking the observations these fixed
hypotheses predict, drawing on those already in the trajectory or
acquiring new ones through non-mutating actions as needed.

Our experiments with BlackSwan support the promise of
refutation-oriented verification. On the most challenging tasks of
AppWorld ([Trivedi et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)), BlackSwan outperforms the
strongest baseline by 14.9%p and 25.2%p in success rate with and without
the backbone model’s thinking mode, respectively. Even without thinking,
BlackSwan outperforms every baseline with thinking by 11.7%p on these
tasks, suggesting that the direction of verification matters more than
the amount of reasoning. Moreover, even without any in-context
demonstration, BlackSwan still outperforms every baseline given three by
9.3%p. Beyond AppWorld, with only its prompts made domain-neutral,
BlackSwan improves over the same agent without verification on WebShop
([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib38)) by 12.7%p. More broadly, our results
suggest that language model agents have an underused capacity to
recognize and self-correct misaligned actions. Our approach elicits this
capacity through a process of falsification: active conjecture and
refutation before execution. Our contributions are:

- $`\bullet`$
  We recast preemptive action verification as a question of direction:
  whether an agent should seek evidence _for_ a proposed action or
  actively seek evidence _against_ it.
- $`\bullet`$
  We introduce BlackSwan, an expect-suspect-test procedure that frames
  each proposed write as a conjecture and executes it only after
  attempted refutation.
- $`\bullet`$
  We suggest that the corrective capacity of agents can be
  systematically elicited at test time, across models and environments,
  even under unfamiliar and task-specific conditions.

## 2 Related Work

#### Task-level information acquisition

One line of work equips agents with missing information before acting. A
line of approaches acquire information from the environment: they rely
on a dedicated exploration phase ([Chen et al., 2026b](#bib.bib3)),
leverage world knowledge models ([Qiao et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)), learn
from synthesized interactions ([SU et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)), or
accumulate reusable artifacts such as manuals ([Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib4)), guidelines ([Fu et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)), workflows
([Wang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib37)), and playbooks ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib41)). Another line of approaches resolve missing
information through clarification queries ([Qian et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18); [Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib42); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib40); [Kobalczyk et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Vijayvargiya
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib30)). Yet both approaches acquire information
before a concrete action exists and therefore cannot target the evidence
needed to test a particular write.

#### Trajectory-based verification and correction

A second line of work intervenes during execution, examining actions
against the trajectory. InferAct ([Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)) infers
the task the trajectory has pursued and approves actions consistent with
the user’s instruction; our expect instead states what the pending write
should do, as a claim to be falsified rather than a basis for approval.
DeAction ([Ning et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)) combines alignment checks
with outcome analysis to detect misaligned actions before execution.
Other methods revise beliefs during execution, reflecting on the current
state relative to the goal ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)) or comparing
expected outcomes with observations once an action has taken effect
([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib32)). Devil’s Advocate ([Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib33)) anticipates failures before execution but checks
them only afterward and recovers by backtracking, presuming
reversibility. These methods reason over trajectories produced under the
very interpretation they aim to correct, and so rarely find evidence
against it before execution.

#### Action-level evidence acquisition

A third line of work obtains evidence beyond the trajectory before an
action executes. Agents may ask the user mid-task ([Chen et al.,
2023](#bib.bib5); [Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib34); [Suri et al.,
2026](#bib.bib27)), which inherits the limits of asking noted above, or
simulate candidate actions with learned world models ([Chae et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)), where evidence remains predicted rather than
observed. Other methods probe the environment directly. EnvProbe ([Song
& Cai, 2026](#bib.bib25)) allocates a probing budget over uncertain or
action-critical beliefs, while AGrail ([Luo et al., 2025](#bib.bib14))
performs action-specific safety checks based on predefined criteria.
ACCORD ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)) intercepts state-changing
actions and uses read-only probes to verify their assumptions about
constraints, entities, and environment states. BlackSwan shares this
access to evidence but differs in how the target of verification is
formed: it first specifies what the action should achieve and what would
falsify that claim, and only then consults the environment. Prior
methods gather evidence to support execution or check predefined
conditions; BlackSwan acquires evidence to challenge the agent’s own
interpretation before a write occurs.

Figure 1: The verification process of BlackSwan. (a) propose drafts a
pending action. (b) expect states its intended outcome. (c) suspect
lists specific ways the action could be wrong. (d) test checks these
suspicions with read-only probes. If any is confirmed, the action is
withheld and reframed using the refuting evidence. The test stage
continues directly from the proposal-stage context window.

## 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification

#### Setup

Given a natural-language task instruction $`u`$, an agent interacts with
an environment through a set of available APIs. At each step
$`t\geq 1`$, the agent generates an action
$`a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid c_{t-1})`$ based on its previous context
$`c_{t-1}=(u,a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1})`$, with $`c_{0}=(u)`$,
and receives an observation $`o_{t}`$, so that
$`c_{t}=c_{t-1}\mathbin{\|}(a_{t},o_{t})`$. We focus on agents that act
through executable code ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib35)): each action
$`a_{t}`$ is a piece of code executed in a persistent interpreter, and
$`o_{t}`$ is the output of its execution (e.g., printed results or
errors). A single action may invoke multiple APIs and bind their results
to variables, which can be reused both later in the same code and in
subsequent actions.

#### Overview

We propose BlackSwan, a refutation-first approach for preemptive action
verification. If an action $`a_{t}`$ invokes at least one state-mutating
API (hereafter, a write), its execution is withheld and the action is
subjected to our conjecture-and-refutation process; otherwise, it is
executed as usual. BlackSwan is inspired by the Popperian view of
conjecture and refutation. Rather than asking if $`a_{t}`$ appears
correct, we ask what observable facts would show $`a_{t}`$ to be wrong,
and test those possibilities before execution.
[Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In Action-level evidence acquisition ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
illustrates our pipeline: expect makes explicit what $`a_{t}`$ claims to
accomplish
([Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Expect: Making the Action’s Intent Explicit ‣ 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents"));
suspect identifies concrete ways in which that claim could be wrong
([Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Suspect: Constructing Potential Falsifiers ‣ 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents"));
and test determines whether those suspicions are supported by
observations of the environment
([Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Test: Trying to Refute the Conjecture ‣ 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")).

### 3.1 Expect: Making the Action’s Intent Explicit

Given the previous context $`c_{t-1}`$ and a proposed write $`a_{t}`$,
the language model predicts what executing $`a_{t}`$ would accomplish
toward fulfilling the user’s task $`u`$:

|     |                                                                |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\kappa_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid c_{t-1},a_{t})\ .`$ |     | (1) |

This prediction $`\kappa_{t}`$ makes explicit the conjecture behind the
proposed action: “executing $`a_{t}`$ should produce $`\kappa_{t}`$ in a
way that advances the user’s task.” It then serves as the claim that the
subsequent suspect stage to challenge.

To make refutation meaningful, we place two constraints on the
prediction. First, $`\kappa_{t}`$ is generated before any new
observation is gathered, so that it cannot be shaped to fit the very
evidence used to test it. Second, $`\kappa_{t}`$ is kept action-local:
it is intended to capture effects attributable to the proposed action
itself, rather than broader outcomes of the overall task execution.

### 3.2 Suspect: Constructing Potential Falsifiers

Given the previous context $`c_{t-1}`$, the proposed write $`a_{t}`$,
and its prediction $`\kappa_{t}`$, the language model identifies
concrete ways in which the conjecture could fail, producing a set of
suspicions

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
S_{t}=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}\}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid c_{t-1},a_{t},\kappa_{t})\ ,
``` |  | (2) |

where each $`s_{i}`$ describes a condition under which executing
$`a_{t}`$ could lead to an effect inconsistent with $`\kappa_{t}`$ or
with the user’s task $`u`$. These suspicions serve as potential
falsifiers, rather than conclusions that the action is wrong. The
subsequent test stage determines from observations whether any of them
actually holds.

Figure 2: Code-grounded suspicions identify testable assumptions that
may change the final answer.

#### Consequential and testable suspicions

Our goal is not to surface every possible error in the prior context
$`c_{t-1}`$ or the proposed write $`a_{t}`$, but only those that (1)
could affect the pending write and (2) can be empirically tested against
observations. A suspicion may concern any part of $`c_{t-1}`$ or
$`a_{t}`$, but its effect must *reach* the write action *through some
concrete code element* $`z_{i}`$ of $`a_{t}`$, such as local variables
and API parameters. To operationalize these requirements, we require the
model to emit each suspicion $`s_{i}`$ together with the corresponding
element as a pair $`(s_{i},z_{i})`$, encouraging it to reason about the
provenance of $`z_{i}`$ and the ambient state surrounding the associated
API call
([Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3.2 Suspect: Constructing Potential Falsifiers ‣ 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")).
As a result, the suspicions focus on consequential failures rather than
on the potentially unbounded set of concerns that never affect the
proposed action, while remaining amenable to empirical testing.

#### Preregistered suspicions

We deliberately separate suspect from test, rather than letting the
model raise and check concerns in a single interleaved loop. When the
two are combined, the model tends to raise only concerns it expects to
resolve easily ([Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)), so the hypotheses end
up shaped by the very observations meant to test them. Instead,
$`S_{t}`$ is generated before any probing, from $`c_{t-1}`$, $`a_{t}`$,
and $`\kappa_{t}`$ alone as in
([2](#S3.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 3.2 Suspect: Constructing Potential Falsifiers ‣ 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")):
at this stage the model reasons only over the proposed code and what has
already been observed, without issuing any new action. Much like
preregistration in empirical science, where hypotheses are committed
before data collection, this fixes what would count as a refutation
before any evidence is gathered. It also holds test accountable: since
test must reach a verdict on every suspicion in $`S_{t}`$, each
registered suspicion is explicitly confirmed, dismissed, or left
unresolved, and none can be silently dropped or reframed once probing
begins.

### 3.3 Test: Trying to Refute the Conjecture

Given the previous context $`c_{t-1}`$, the proposed write $`a_{t}`$,
and the potential falsifiers $`S_{t}`$, the language model attempts to
resolve each suspicion $`s_{i}\in S_{t}`$ using observations from the
environment. Rather than judging a suspicion from the proposed code and
reasoning alone, the model must resolve each $`s_{i}`$ from observable
evidence: it can revisit observations already available in $`c_{t-1}`$
or acquire new ones as needed by issuing non-mutating actions.

#### Probing and verdict

The pending write $`a_{t}`$ is appended to $`c_{t-1}`$ as an unexecuted
action, after which the agent receives an observation $`o_{t}`$ that
presents $`S_{t}`$ as suspicions to resolve, yielding
$`c_{t}=c_{t-1}\mathbin{\|}(a_{t},o_{t})`$. Concretely, $`o_{t}`$ is a
user-role message of the form “I’m suspicious of executing this action
for the following reasons: $`S_{t}`$. Please verify whether each of them
is the case.” The agent then continues from $`c_{t}`$. At each probing
step $`k\geq 1`$, it either issues a non-mutating action
$`a_{t+k}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid c_{t+k-1})`$, whose observation $`o_{t+k}`$
extends the context as
$`c_{t+k}=c_{t+k-1}\mathbin{\|}(a_{t+k},o_{t+k})`$, or emits a verdict
$`v_{t}\colon S_{t}\to\{\textnormal{{true}},\textnormal{{false}},\textnormal{{deferred}}\}`$
that resolves each suspicion as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle v_{t}(s_{i})=\begin{cases}\textnormal{{true}}&\text{if observations confirm }s_{i}\ ,\\
\textnormal{{false}}&\text{if observations dismiss }s_{i}\ ,\\
\textnormal{{deferred}}&\text{otherwise}\ ,\end{cases}`$ |  | (3) |

where deferred covers suspicions that probing can neither confirm nor
dismiss, typically because they depend on the outcome of executing
$`a_{t}`$ itself (e.g., a transient network failure during an API call).
Testing ends when the agent emits $`v_{t}`$ at some step $`K`$. Unlike
the probing actions, $`v_{t}`$ is not appended, leaving the context at
$`c_{t+K-1}`$.

#### Acting on the verdict

The verdict determines whether the pending write is released as follows:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\forall s_{i}\in S_{t}\colon\;v_{t}(s_{i})=\textnormal{{false}}\lor v_{t}(s_{i})=\textnormal{{deferred}}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow\quad\text{execute }a_{t},`$ |  | (4a) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\exists s_{i}\in S_{t}\colon\;v_{t}(s_{i})=\textnormal{{true}}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow\quad\text{withhold }a_{t}\text{ and draft }a_{t}^{\prime}.`$ |  | (4b) |

In
([4a](#S3.E4.1 "Equation 4a ‣ Equation 4 ‣ Acting on the verdict ‣ 3.3 Test: Trying to Refute the Conjecture ‣ 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")),
the proposed action $`a_{t}`$ has survived every refutation attempt;
suspicions labeled deferred do not block execution because they cannot
be resolved without observing the effect of $`a_{t}`$. Thus, $`a_{t}`$
is reissued as the next action, $`a_{t+K}=a_{t}`$, this time executed.
In
([4b](#S3.E4.2 "Equation 4b ‣ Equation 4 ‣ Acting on the verdict ‣ 3.3 Test: Trying to Refute the Conjecture ‣ 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")),
a single confirmed suspicion suffices to withhold $`a_{t}`$, as the
action is no longer consistent with the conjecture it was intended to
fulfill. The agent drafts a replacement $`a_{t}^{\prime}`$ from
$`c_{t+K-1}`$ with $`v_{t}`$ provided as additional context (e.g., as an
assistant prefill). If $`a_{t}^{\prime}`$ is another write action, it
undergoes the same expect-suspect-test procedure. In either case, the
context then grows as before,
$`c_{t+K}=c_{t+K-1}\mathbin{\|}(a_{t+K},o_{t+K})`$.

## 4 Experiments

Unless otherwise stated, all methods use the official FP8 checkpoint of
Qwen3.5-27B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib20)) as the underlying model,
following Accord ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)).

#### Benchmarks

Our primary benchmark is AppWorld ([Trivedi et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)),
where an agent with access to 457 APIs across 9 simulated applications
completes user requests by discovering and invoking the ones it needs.
AppWorld captures key challenges of assistant deployment: agents must
discover persistent user data, avoid unintended state changes, and
account for irreversible writes. Tasks are grouped into scenarios of
three similar variants that differ in user and environment states. On
the normal (168 tasks) and challenge (417 tasks) test splits, we report
the two official metrics: *task goal completion* (TGC), the fraction of
tasks that pass all of their unit tests (8 on average, up to 22), and
*scenario goal completion* (SGC), the fraction of scenarios in which all
three tasks pass. We additionally evaluate on WebShop ([Yao et al.,
2022](#bib.bib38)) and ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib24)) to
show that BlackSwan generalizes to environments with different action
spaces.

#### Baselines

ReAct ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib39)) interleaves reasoning with code
actions ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib35)) and executes every action
immediately, serving as the unguarded reference on which BlackSwan and
the other baselines are built. ACE ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib41))
enriches the agent’s knowledge of its environment with a playbook of
strategies and pitfalls distilled from training tasks.²² 2 We run its
released implementation
([https://github.com/ace-agent/ace](https://github.com/ace-agent/ace)).
Comparing BlackSwan against it tests whether knowledge supplied in
advance suffices, or whether erroneous mutations also stem from
task-specific facts that it cannot anticipate. Accord ([Jiang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)) admits each write once revisited or newly probed
observations support its required conditions.³³ 3 As no implementation
of Accord was publicly available as of September 25, 2026, we
reimplemented it from the paper, resolving unspecified design choices as
consistently with its description as possible
([Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Reproducing Accord ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")).
As an instance of the confirmation-oriented view, it isolates the
direction in which verification looks: Accord seeks evidence for the
write, whereas BlackSwan seeks evidence against it.

#### Overall performance

[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
shows that BlackSwan achieves the highest performance on AppWorld,
regardless of whether the underlying model’s thinking mode is on or off.
With thinking on, it improves over the strongest baseline in each column
(underlined) by 6.8 TGC and 8.6 SGC points on the normal split, and by
14.9 and 19.2 points on the challenge split. Without thinking, the
corresponding margins are 7.9 and 10.1 points on the normal split, and
25.2 and 20.2 points on the challenge split. As ACE and Accord represent
the two prevailing responses to the information gap, namely knowledge
acquired in advance and confirmation-oriented verification, these
margins suggest that subjecting each proposed action to conjecture and
refutation resolves errors that both often leave unaddressed.

#### Robustness under distribution shift

Figure 5: AppWorld results by difficulty, from 1 (easiest) to 3
(hardest).

Moving from the normal to the challenge split in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents"),
the TGC of BlackSwan drops by only 3.6 points with thinking on and 2.6
without, whereas even the most robust baseline, Accord ^(†) with
thinking on, drops by 11.7 points. ACE and Accord improve over ReAct on
both splits but drop nearly as much as ReAct. That is, knowledge
acquired in advance and confirmation-oriented verification raise
performance, but do not reduce the drop on the challenge split. For ACE,
this is because its playbook is distilled from training tasks, none of
which involve the applications required by the challenge split. The gap
is also evident in SGC: on the challenge split, BlackSwan completes
entire scenarios more often than any baseline completes individual
tasks, both with thinking on (72.4 SGC versus at most 69.8 TGC) and off
(65.0 versus 56.3). The gap also widens *within* the challenge split.
Across AppWorld’s difficulty levels
([Figure 5](#S4.F5 "In Robustness under distribution shift ‣ 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")),
our margin over Accord grows to +21.5 points at the hardest, which
requires orchestrating the largest number of API calls.

#### Gains beyond reasoning and demonstrations

BlackSwan outperforms the baselines even when they are given more
reasoning or more in-context supervision. In
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents"),
BlackSwan without thinking outperforms every baseline with thinking,
including Accord^(†), on all four metrics.
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
varies the number of in-context demonstrations from zero to three, with
thinking off. Additional demonstrations benefit the baselines, most
notably Accord on the challenge split, whose TGC rises from about 55 to
69 points. BlackSwan, in contrast, stays within about 3 points across
demonstration counts and, even without any demonstration, outperforms
every baseline given three. These results suggest that the verification
procedure of BlackSwan offers benefits that additional reasoning or
demonstrations do not readily provide.

#### Other backbone models

[Table 1(a)](#S4.T1.st1 "In Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Transfer to Other Models and Environments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
repeats the AppWorld comparison with three further models: the dense
Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib28)) and two large
mixture-of-experts models, MiniMax M2.7 ([Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib2)) and GLM-5.3-Flash ([GLM-5-Team et al.,
2026](#bib.bib8)). With every model, BlackSwan outperforms both
baselines on all metrics and splits. In contrast, Accord improves over
ReAct in TGC only with MiniMax M2.7. With GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3-4B, it
falls below ReAct on both splits, by up to 8.3 points with Qwen3-4B
(14.9 versus 23.2 on the normal split). These results suggest that the
benefit of confirmation-oriented verification depends on the model,
whereas our conjecture and refutation improves performance with every
model we test.

#### Other environments

[Table 1(b)](#S4.T1.st2 "In Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Transfer to Other Models and Environments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
evaluates BlackSwan on two benchmarks with different action spaces:
WebShop, where the agent navigates an online store through search and
click actions (e.g., click\[Buy Now\]), and ALFWorld, where it acts in a
household through text commands (e.g., take apple 1 from countertop 2).
BlackSwan runs the same, proposed procedure as on AppWorld, with only
its prompts made domain-neutral. On WebShop, it improves the success
rate over ReAct by 12.7 points and over Harness-R1 ([Shao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)) by 8.8. On ALFWorld, it improves over ReAct by 0.7
points and over Accord by 0.2. However, Accord here uses a procedure
designed specifically for ALFWorld, unlike ours. Note that the
applicable baselines differ across benchmarks; for example, Accord is
defined over write APIs, which WebShop does not expose in the same form.
The results in
[Table 1(b)](#S4.T1.st2 "In Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Transfer to Other Models and Environments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
therefore test whether BlackSwan transfers to other environments, rather
than replicating the comparison in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents").

## 5 Analysis

|              |            |          |            |
|--------------|------------|----------|------------|
|              | Suspicions |          |            |
| Orientation  | Explicit   | Implicit | $`\Delta`$ |
| Refutation   | 81.6       | 72.7     | $`8.9`$    |
| Confirmation | 76.0       | 72.6     | $`3.4`$    |
| $`\Delta`$   | $`5.6`$    | $`0.1`$  |            |

Table 2: Verification orientation and externalization, varied
separately.

#### Ablation

[Table 2](#S5.T2 "In 5 Analysis ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
varies two design choices of BlackSwan separately on test-challenge with
thinking off: whether the verifier asks how the proposed action could be
wrong (refutation) or what it requires to hold (confirmation), and
whether the potential falsifiers are written out and fixed before
testing (explicit) or formed by the agent internally as it tests
(implicit). For reference, Accord, which conceptually corresponds to
confirmation with implicit suspicions, reaches $`69.3\pm 1.8`$% TGC. We
find that the two choices are effective only in combination. Refutation
improves TGC by 5.6 points when suspicions are explicit but by 0.1 when
they are implicit, and fixing suspicions in advance improves TGC by 8.9
points under refutation but by 3.4 under confirmation. This supports the
preregistration of suspicions in
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Suspect: Constructing Potential Falsifiers ‣ 3 Conjecture and Refutation for Preemptive Verification ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents"):
asking how an action could be wrong improves verification when the
resulting suspicions are fixed before testing.

#### Computational cost

[Figure 6](#S4.F6 "In Other environments ‣ 4.2 Transfer to Other Models and Environments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
compares each agent with ReAct on the same backbone. Accord costs
1.7–3.0$`\times`$ as much as ReAct without consistently improving
completion, and falls below it on Qwen3-4B ($`0.71\times`$). BlackSwan
lies on the frontier on every backbone: on Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3-4B, and
MiniMax M2.7, it completes 1.39–2.25$`\times`$ as many tasks at
1.5–9.4$`\times`$ the cost, gaining most on the weakest, Qwen3-4B. On
GLM-5.3-flash, where ReAct already completes 77.5% of tasks, BlackSwan
gains less but is the only agent to improve. Both cost measures rank the
agents identically, so the comparison is insensitive to cache reuse.

#### Failures reduced by verification

Omission, a required change that the agent never makes, is the most
frequent error for every agent, and it is the error that verifying
proposed writes is least able to see, since no write for it is ever
proposed. Both Accord and BlackSwan reduce every kind of error relative
to ReAct, and BlackSwan reduces each more than Accord. Per 100 tasks,
BlackSwan leaves 16.1 required changes undone, against 24.9 for Accord,
a reduction of 35%; it also makes 39% fewer wrong values and 26% fewer
collateral changes. In absolute terms, the largest reduction is in
omission, which calls for an explanation.

#### Burden of proof

The two verifiers place the burden of proof differently. Accord rejects
an action only when an observation confirms a violation and otherwise is
told to “default to APPROVE” ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)), placing
the burden on stopping the action; asking what would show the action
wrong places it on executing it. Two consequences follow (right). First,
BlackSwan gathers more new evidence: per verification, it makes 0.76
reads the agent had not already made on completed tasks and 0.91 on
failed ones, against 0.33 and 0.26 for Accord. As a result, no
verification read reached the faulted application in 53.1% of Accord’s
failures, against 11.3% for BlackSwan. Second, the verdict of BlackSwan
tracks the outcome. On the action that ends the task, the last chance to
catch an omission, BlackSwan rejects it in 20.7% of failed tasks and
2.9% of successful ones, whereas Accord rejects it in 1.8% and 4.1%.
This reversal is specific to that gate: over all verifications,
BlackSwan rejects 54.4% of actions against 8.4% for Accord, and both
reject more often on failed trials.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced a refutation-oriented approach to preemptive action
verification, where agents actively seek evidence against proposed
state-mutating actions before execution. BlackSwan operationalizes this
idea with an expect-suspect-test procedure that fixes testable
suspicions before gathering evidence. On AppWorld, BlackSwan achieves
84.7 TGC and 72.4 SGC on the challenge split, improving over the
strongest baseline by 14.9 and 19.2 points, with even larger TGC gains
when thinking is disabled; it also remains stronger without
demonstrations than baselines given three. The gains are consistent
across four backbones and transfer to WebShop and ALFWorld, while
ablations show that generating suspicions helps substantially only when
they are fixed before testing. Overall, the results suggest that agents
have an underused capacity to recognize and correct misaligned actions
at test time through active conjecture and refutation before execution.

#### Limitations and future work

Refutation cannot resolve genuine ambiguity: when user instructions
admit multiple plausible interpretations, it may repeatedly surface the
same unresolved issue across successive proposals, increasing
verification cost. A natural extension is to treat such recurring
suspicions as a signal of ambiguity and escalate them to the user for
clarification.

### AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools (Claude Code) to implement
methods, to design and give feedback on experiments, to propose and
refine hypotheses, to support qualitative analysis of agent
trajectories, and to interpret results. We have not used generative AI
tools to generate synthetic data sets, to develop the conceptual
framework, to assist with translation, or to clean or reformat data
sets, and formulating mathematical claims or proofs is not applicable to
this work. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. We take responsibility
for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts
produced with the aid of generative AI.

### Ethics statement

All experiments run in the simulated environments of AppWorld ([Trivedi
et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)), WebShop ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib38)),
and ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib24)). They involve no
human subjects and no real personal data, as the users in AppWorld are
fictitious. Pre-execution verification reduces but does not eliminate
erroneous agent actions, so agents acting on real accounts still require
further safeguards. Models accessed through a commercial API received
only benchmark content.

### Reproducibility statement

Implementation details are given in the appendix: our agent
([Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation details of BlackSwan ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents"))
and its prompts
([Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B BlackSwan prompts ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")),
the reproduction of Accord and its prompts
([Appendices C](#A3 "Appendix C Reproducing Accord ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
and [D](#A4 "Appendix D Accord prompts ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")),
and cost measurement
([Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Cost measurement ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")).

## Appendix A Implementation details of BlackSwan

[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Appendix A Implementation details of BlackSwan ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
gives the loop of BlackSwan on one task, and
[Table 3](#A1.T3 "In Context ‣ Appendix A Implementation details of BlackSwan ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
its limits. BlackSwan is a code agent in the style of ReAct: each step
drafts one Python cell $`c`$ and runs it. $`h`$ is the history the model
sees, and $`h\oplus(\cdot)`$ appends turns to it. Each call marked with
a prompt reads $`h`$ but adds nothing to it; only the appends in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Appendix A Implementation details of BlackSwan ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
do.

1: instruction $`x`$, model $`M`$

2: $`h\leftarrow`$ the ReAct prompt with $`x`$; $`T\leftarrow\emptyset`$
$`\triangleright`$ word–endpoint tables

3: repeat

4:   for $`a=0,\ldots,3`$ do $`\triangleright`$ at most 3 redrafts

5:    $`c\leftarrow\textsc{Draft}(M,h)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Prompt ;
form rules

6:    if $`c`$ only reads then break

7:    $`e\leftarrow\textsc{Expect}(M,h,c)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Prompt

8:    $`S\leftarrow\textsc{Suspect}(M,h,c,e,\textsc{Anatomy}(c),T)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Prompts ,

9:    if $`S=\emptyset`$ then break

10:    $`(P,V)\leftarrow\textsc{Test}(M,h,c,S)`$ $`\triangleright`$
Prompt

11:    $`h\leftarrow h\oplus(c,S,P,V)`$ $`\triangleright`$ probes $`P`$,
verdicts $`V`$

12:    if no verdict in $`V`$ is *confirmed* then break

13:   end for

14:   $`o\leftarrow`$ run $`c`$; $`h\leftarrow h\oplus(c,o)`$
$`\triangleright`$ the last draft runs even if blocked

15:   if $`c`$ lists a new app $`u`$’s endpoints then
$`T\leftarrow T\cup\textsc{Ground}(M,h,u,x)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Prompt

16: until $`c`$ calls complete_task

Algorithm 1 BlackSwan on one task.

#### Draft

Three rules check the form of a drafted cell. A cell that calls an
endpoint whose documentation the agent has not read is replaced by that
lookup; a cell that reads an endpoint’s documentation before the app’s
endpoint list is replaced by the list; and a cell that calls
complete_task together with other code is drafted again. A cell *only
reads* when every API call in it is a GET request, a documentation
lookup, or login; a cell with no API call is verified.

#### Verification

Anatomy is a static analysis of the cell: its variable bindings and API
calls in evaluation order, each call with every parameter, including
those left at their documented defaults. On a cell that calls
complete_task, Suspect asks instead what part of the task is not done
yet (Prompt ), at most twice per task. Test judges all suspicions
together. At each turn the model either writes a probe, which the
harness runs and answers with its output, or ends with a verdict for
every suspicion: *confirmed*, *dismissed*, or *deferred*. A probe may
only read. A probe that makes the cell’s own write defers every verdict,
since only running the cell can settle it; a probe that makes any other
write is refused, and the model is asked again. Only a confirmed
suspicion blocks the cell. The verdicts then end $`h`$, so the next
draft continues from them.

#### Context

Before each model call, while $`h`$ exceeds the context budget, the
harness shortens its cell outputs one step at a time, oldest first;
every value it clips stays retrievable from the environment.

| Item | Limit |
|----|----|
| Word–endpoint table | once per app, at most 8 entries |
| Expect | one expectation, at most 500 characters |
| Suspect | at most 5 suspicions, each at most 1,000 characters |
| Test | at most 50 read-only probes per verification; grounds at most 400 characters |
| Redrafts of a blocked cell | at most 3 per step |
| Decoding | temperature 0, at most 8,192 generated tokens per call |

Table 3: Limits of BlackSwan in the runs of
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents").

## Appendix B BlackSwan prompts

BlackSwan runs the same stages on all three benchmarks. The prompt the
agent starts from and the API it reads are the benchmark’s own. The
verification prompts are AppWorld’s on ALFWorld as well; on WebShop,
Suspect and Test also state how the shop works, Suspect words two of its
five kinds for a shop, and Test names the shop’s read endpoints and
defers two kinds of suspicion (Prompts and ). Values filled in at run
time are shown in angle brackets; limits are those of the reported runs.

### B.1 AppWorld

The agent drafts each action on AppWorld’s official ReAct prompt with
its one demonstration, to which it adds the turns of Prompt . When it
lists an app’s endpoints, it answers Prompt once for that app. Each
drafted action that writes to the environment then goes through Expect
(Prompt ), Suspect (Prompt , or Prompt when the action ends the task),
and Test (Prompts and ), and the agent’s next turn begins with the
verdicts (Prompt ).

\- Be precise about which objects, values, or parts of the user's

Prompt 3: Expect.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Before that cell runs, argue against yourself. What could make what you

In the order it would run, that cell binds these variables and makes

\<the cell's variables and API calls, every parameter included\>

Look for failures of these kinds:

1. \*\*The wrong thing.\*\* The objects this acts on may not be the ones
the task asked for — a name that merely looks right, an id read off the
wrong record.

2. \*\*Not all of them.\*\* The task may name a set or an amount this
cell does not cover. If it acts on some members, say what would show
there are others it missed.

3. \*\*The wrong value or operation.\*\* The arguments, quantities, or
the endpoint itself may not be what the request means, even when the
target is right.

4. \*\*Hidden state.\*\* Something already in the environment may change
the outcome — what is in the cart, what the account already holds, what
an earlier cell left behind.

5. \*\*The task's words.\*\* The part of the task this code carries out
may ask for something the code does not do: an endpoint whose
description matches those words more closely than the one it calls, or a
condition, an amount or a second action in those words that the code
leaves out.

When you read the apps' endpoints, you matched the task's words to these
endpoints:

\<the word–endpoint table\>

Each entry is one way it could fail, in terms that a read of the
environment could settle, and under 1000 characters. Say what it is
about as its \`ref\`: one of the \`ref\` values listed above, exactly as
written there. Give EVERY doubt you actually have, up to 5 — the number
is not fixed, and the shape below is not a hint at how many. If you
genuinely see none, answer with an empty list.

Answer in exactly one fenced \`\`\`json\`\`\` block:

\`\`\`json

\[{"doubt": "\<one way it could turn out wrong\>", "ref": "\<one of the

Go through the task's words one by one — every action it asks for, every

\<the suspicions, numbered\>

—

Do your best to gather thorough and sufficient evidence to determine
whether each suspicion should be confirmed or dismissed. Investigate
them seriously in either direction: do not try to defend the proposed

\*\*Do not treat plausibility, possibility, or expectation as
evidence.\*\* When the current evidence does not decisively settle a
suspicion, actively use evidence-gathering probes to obtain observations
that can. Choose probes for their ability to distinguish the
possibilities, and keep probing until you have concrete evidence or no

Answer with exactly either a \`\`\`python\`\`\` or \`\`\`json\`\`\`
block.

If more evidence is needed, return one \`\`\`python\`\`\` block
containing an evidence-gathering probe:

When you can judge, return one \`\`\`json\`\`\` block covering \*\*\<the
suspicions' numbers\>\*\* — those are the ones an observation can

\`\`\`json

characters at most\>"}}

\`\`\`

probe can settle. If a useful probe could still distinguish the
possibilities, probe instead of deferring.

A suspicion about the task's words — another endpoint, or a part of the
task not done — is confirmed only by a line you quote as the grounds: an
endpoint's description from the API docs, or an Output line showing the

Prompt 14: ALFWorld: the game’s API documentation as it enters the
agent’s context. Each api_docs cell is followed by its Output, verbatim
from the runs: the list of the game’s endpoints, one per command, then
the specification of each. The agent never read the specification of
close in these runs; it is shown as the environment returns it.

## Appendix C Reproducing Accord

Accord ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)) verifies an agent’s action
before it runs. A second model, the grounding agent, receives the task,
the agent’s trajectory and the code the agent is about to execute; it
may issue read-only calls to observe the environment, and it returns
APPROVE or REJECT together with a note of what it observed. On REJECT
the code is discarded, the note is appended to the agent’s history, and
the agent drafts again. The paper releases no code, so we re-implemented
the method from its description, its Algorithm 1 and its prompt
appendix. This section records what the paper fixes, what it leaves open
and the choice we made in each case, the prompt and model configuration,
and how our numbers compare with the reported ones.

#### What the paper specifies

The backbone and its decoding (Qwen3.5-27B in FP8, temperature 0); the
grounding-agent prompt (its Appendix A.5, reproduced verbatim in
§[D](#A4 "Appendix D Accord prompts ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents"));
the inputs to that prompt, namely the pending code, the context and the
task; three policy items added to the agent’s instructions, numbered
(10) to (12) in the paper: inspect raw content before writing parsing
logic, re-examine the API specification when a response is not as
expected, and list the APIs of every app before starting the task; and
the control flow of Algorithm 1: an action that calls a sensitive API is
withheld, the grounding agent observes and decides, and on REJECT the
attempt is removed from the agent’s history and the grounding agent’s
evidence is appended in its place.

#### What it leaves open, and what we chose

[Table 5](#A3.T5 "In What it leaves open, and what we chose ‣ Appendix C Reproducing Accord ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
lists the remaining decisions and our choice for each.

|  Left open by the paper |  Our choice |
|----|----|
|  Which calls are sensitive |  Every endpoint whose HTTP method is not GET (POST, PATCH, DELETE), plus supervisor.complete_task. The set is computed from the code before execution, by a syntax-tree walk over apis.\<app\>.\<endpoint\>( calls. |
|  Grounding-agent model |  The same model and decoding as the agent. |
|  Grounding-agent memory |  One chat per task, kept across verifications. Each verification after the first shows only the steps taken since the previous one. |
|  Where observations run |  In the agent’s own namespace, so the grounding agent can read the agent’s variables. Write endpoints raise instead of executing, and the observation code runs inside a function so that it cannot rebind the agent’s variables. |
|  Observation budget |  Five observation rounds per verification. A reply with neither code nor a decision is answered with a one-line reminder of the output format and costs a round. When the budget is exhausted the decision is forced to APPROVE. |
|  Rejections per task |  Three. After the third, a REJECT is ignored and the code executes. |
|  Message on REJECT |  The OBSERVE note, appended to the last user turn as “Your previous code was NOT executed. Before executing sensitive API calls, the environment was observed and the following was reported: … Revise your code accordingly.” (§[D](#A4 "Appendix D Accord prompts ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")). The discarded attempt is removed, as Algorithm 1 specifies; the wording around the note is ours. |
|  Layout of the grounding input |  Four labeled blocks: the task instruction, the agent trajectory, the code about to execute, and the triggered sensitive APIs with their HTTP methods (§[D](#A4 "Appendix D Accord prompts ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")). |
|  Policy item (12) |  The item tells the agent to begin by calling show_api_descriptions(app_name=""), which lists the APIs of every app. Left to the model, it repeats this call until the context is full, so we issue the call for it as the first step of every task and let the environment answer the empty name with the list of all apps. |
|  Step limit |  None. An episode ends when the agent calls complete_task or when the context limit is reached. |

Table 5: Decisions the paper leaves open and the choice taken in our
implementation of Accord.

#### Base prompt and demonstrations

The paper names no base prompt for the main agent, and its policy items
are numbered from (10). We use the ACE generator prompt ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib41)) with its seed playbook, whose key instructions end at
(8), and insert the three policy items after the last key instruction.
AppWorld’s official prompt, the other public candidate, ends its
demonstration by passing an answer to complete_task, and with it the
agent passes answers on tasks that expect none. The ACE prompt carries
three demonstrations. For
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents"),
where every method receives one demonstration, we keep only the first:
the other two demonstration blocks are removed, and the playbook, the
key instructions, and the task turn are unchanged.
[Table 6](#A3.T6 "In Result ‣ Appendix C Reproducing Accord ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
reports both versions, and
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.1 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
varies the number of demonstrations for every method.

#### Backbone and decoding

Qwen3.5-27B in FP8 at temperature 0, for both the agent and the
grounding agent. We report Accord with thinking on and with thinking
off, since the paper marks only its 9B model as non-thinking. No cap is
placed on generated tokens other than the 262k-token context. As for
every other agent in this paper, observations are truncated to 20k
characters and the history to 400k characters.

#### Evaluation

AppWorld test-normal (168 tasks) and test-challenge (417 tasks), scored
by the official evaluator: TGC is the fraction of tasks whose checks all
pass, and SGC the fraction of scenarios whose tasks all pass. Each row
is the mean and sample standard deviation over three runs.

#### Result

[Table 6](#A3.T6 "In Result ‣ Appendix C Reproducing Accord ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
sets our runs against the paper’s Table 1. With the three-demonstration
prompt, our reproduction meets the reported test-challenge numbers with
thinking on (71.9 against 69.8 TGC; 59.0 against 53.2 SGC) and falls
short on test-normal by 4.3 TGC points (77.2 against 81.5), more than
the run-to-run spread. The budgets, the memory of the grounding agent,
and the base prompt are all unstated in the paper, so we cannot
attribute the gap to any one choice in
[Table 5](#A3.T5 "In What it leaves open, and what we chose ‣ Appendix C Reproducing Accord ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents").
With one demonstration, Accord completes more test-normal tasks (79.4
TGC) and fewer test-challenge tasks (63.5 TGC) than with three. The
budgets rarely bind: in the first one-demonstration test-challenge run
with thinking, the grounding agent was invoked 2,916 times over the 417
tasks and rejected 171 actions; the observation budget ran out 9 times,
and the rejection cap overrode 3 rejections.

|  |  |  | test-normal |  | test-challenge |  |

USER:

You are a verification agent. Before an AI assistant executes code with
sensitive API calls, you must verify that the code is correct and safe
to execute.

\## Core principle: Observe, then verify, then decide

Your primary tool is \*\*observation\*\* — executing read-only Python
code to inspect the actual environment state. Do NOT reason about
correctness from the code alone. Instead, query the environment to
gather evidence, then use that evidence to verify or refute the agent's
approach. Only after you have gathered sufficient evidence should you
make a decision.

\## How to observe

Write read-only Python code in \`\`\`python …\`\`\` blocks. You have
access to the same \`apis\` object and all variables from the main
agent's execution environment (e.g., access_token, results from prior
steps).

\*\*What you can call in observations:\*\*

\- Any read-only API (write operations will be blocked)

\- API documentation:
\`apis.api_docs.show_api_descriptions(app_name=…)\` and
\`apis.api_docs.show_api_doc(app_name=…, api_name=…)\` to check API
specifications

\*\*Leverage the trajectory before observing:\*\*

You have access to the agent's full execution trajectory, including all
intermediate print outputs and API responses. Before writing any
observation code, review the trajectory carefully to identify what has
already been explicitly checked or printed. If the trajectory already
contains the evidence you need (e.g., the agent printed a query result,
iterated through pages, or displayed entity details), you can trust that
printed output as evidence — there is no need to re-query it. Only
observe what is \*\*missing or ambiguous\*\* in the trajectory.

\*\*Observation strategies (apply only to gaps not already covered by
the trajectory):\*\*

\- \*\*Re-query the data source\*\*: If the agent operated on data it
never actually inspected in the trajectory, re-fetch the raw data
yourself to verify that the agent's logic matches the real data
structure and content.

\- \*\*Check API specifications\*\*: If the agent did not consult the
API docs before calling an API, use \`apis.api_docs.show_api_doc()\` to
verify it used correct parameter names, types, and values.

\- \*\*Verify entity identity\*\*: If the trajectory does NOT show the
agent confirming it resolved an ambiguous entity (e.g., which "John" or
which "note"), observe the environment to verify.

\- \*\*Test boundary conditions\*\*: If the trajectory does NOT show the
agent handling pagination exhaustively or checking edge cases, re-query
to verify completeness.

\## Verification checklist

For each verification item below, use observation to gather evidence
before making a judgment.

\### 1. Constraint satisfaction

Re-read the task instruction word by word. Extract and QUOTE every
explicit constraint verbatim (e.g., recipients, amounts, dates,
conditions, filters, set operations like "X that are in Y"). Do NOT
paraphrase — copy the exact wording. Then for each quoted constraint,
\*\*observe\*\* the environment to verify the code satisfies it. Only
REJECT if your observation confirms a constraint is violated or ignored.

\### 2. Ambiguity resolution

Identify any ambiguity in the agent's actions — such as unverified
entity references (e.g., which "John"? which "meeting"?), assumed IDs,
or implicit choices made without evidence. Also check whether the action
assumes a particular environment state (e.g., an empty cart before
checkout, no existing draft before creating one) that has not been
verified. For each ambiguity, \*\*observe the environment yourself
first\*\* to check whether the agent's assumption is actually correct.
Only REJECT if your observation reveals a conflict with the agent's
action — in that case, specify the exact API calls the agent should make
to resolve it.

\## Workflow

1. Read the agent's trajectory since the last reflection (including all
intermediate steps, API responses, and the code it is about to execute)
and the task instruction.

2. Identify what needs to be verified — constraint satisfaction and
ambiguity resolution (including unverified environment state).

3. \*\*Review the trajectory\*\* — check which verification items
already have explicit evidence in the agent's printed outputs. Note
these as "covered by trajectory".

4. \*\*Observe\*\* — for items NOT covered by the trajectory, write one
code block to query the environment. Wait for the result.

5. Repeat step 4 as needed until you have enough evidence for all items.

6. \*\*Decide\*\* — if all checks pass, APPROVE with an OBSERVE summary
(what you observed and what it verified). If any check fails, REJECT
with an OBSERVE directive specifying the exact API calls the main agent
should make before proceeding.

\## Output format

When observing (one code block per message):

\`\`\`python

\# Describe what you are checking

print(…)

\`\`\`

When deciding (only after sufficient observation):

DECISION: APPROVE

OBSERVE: \<what you observed (which APIs you called, what data you
checked) and what it verified (which constraints and assumptions were
confirmed)\>

or

DECISION: REJECT

OBSERVE: \<specify the API calls the main agent should make and what
information to pay attention to — do NOT include your own judgment or
conclusion\>

\## Key rules

\- NEVER output observation code and a DECISION in the same message.
Observe first, wait for results, then decide in a separate message.

\- Write one code block per observation step. Do not combine multiple
unrelated checks.

\- You may take multiple observation steps before deciding.

\- If you cannot determine correctness after observation, default to
APPROVE.

\- Do NOT attempt to fix or rewrite the code. Only APPROVE or REJECT.

## Appendix E Cost measurement

#### Token counts

For every model call, the serving engine reports the number of input
tokens it received and the number of tokens it generated: SGLang for the
Qwen backbones, which we serve ourselves, and the API provider
(OpenRouter) for GLM-5.3-flash and MiniMax M2.7. We sum both counts over
all model calls of an episode, including the verification calls of our
agent and the grounding calls of Accord. Input tokens count every token
sent on every call, including a prefix that a serving cache could reuse;
generated tokens include thinking tokens. For each task we average over
the runs of a configuration, and then average over the tasks of the
split. When a task has more than one trial in a run (a re-run after a
lost worker), we use the latest.

#### Cost measures

The first measure is the number of generated tokens per task. The second
prices input and generated tokens per task at one common price, the
OpenRouter list price of Qwen3.5-27B (\$0.195 per million input tokens
and \$1.56 per million generated tokens, September 2026), so that the
measure reflects how many tokens a harness uses rather than which model
is cheap.
[Figure 6](#S4.F6 "In Other environments ‣ 4.2 Transfer to Other Models and Environments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
divides both measures, and the task goal completion, by those of ReAct
with thinking on the same backbone. An agent lies on the frontier of its
backbone if no other agent on the same backbone costs no more and
completes more tasks.

#### All measured points

[Table 7](#A5.T7 "In All measured points ‣ Appendix E Cost measurement ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
lists every point on both test splits, including Qwen3-30B-A3B, which
[Figure 6](#S4.F6 "In Other environments ‣ 4.2 Transfer to Other Models and Environments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")

## Appendix F Qualitative examples

[Tables 8](#A6.T8 "In Appendix F Qualitative examples ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
and [9](#A6.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix F Qualitative examples ‣ Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents")
show two tasks from the AppWorld test-challenge split, run with
Qwen3.5-27B and thinking off: Accord with the ACE prompt’s three
demonstrations on the left and BlackSwan on the right, one run each. On
both tasks the two agents take the same first steps and propose the same
action. Accord’s grounding agent reads the environment to confirm the
action and approves it once what it reads agrees with the action.
BlackSwan instead asks what would make the action wrong and reads for
that. In the first task it finds a third cancellation, worded without
the search terms; in the second it finds that a returned wrench has the
````
